en: Udīcya Śyāmilaka: *Pādatāḍitaka* The *Pādatāḍitaka*, composed by the illustrious great poet Śyāmilaka.
(At the end of the *nāndī*, the *sūtradhāra* enters.
(*Sūtradhāra*) He by whom the wrath of Śambhu was honored in the fire of his eye through the sacrifice of his own body...
(b) He whose instruction the gods, including Indra, wear upon their heads like a garland;
(c) may that Kāma protect you—he who has the side-glances from the eyes of beautiful women as his bow;
(d) he whose arrows are the objects of the senses, which captivate and pierce the minds of even ascetics.
Moreover:
(a) while gazing at the Queen with a raised eyebrow and a smile, his hand placed upon her breast;
(b) while being saluted by Nandin along with the Gaṇapatis, whose voices were choked with terror.
(c) May Puṣpaketu protect you— he who, with his right hand placed upon the hump of the Bull, the lord of beasts,
(d) whose external instrument was stolen by the enraged Śambhu, but not his power.
Having thus bowed my head to the noble sirs, I inform you that we intend to perform the *bhāṇa* named *Pādatāḍitaka*, the composition of the noble Śyāmilaka.
[66] We wish to favor the diligent labor of this poet by bestowing our attention upon it; for why?
(a) "Let this word here not be thus; let this other be otherwise";
(b) "This has been done; by this composition, a great meaning has been established."
(c) Thus, whatever effort the poet exerts in his mind at the commencement of a poem, (d) that [effort] the tears in the eyes and the bristling of the hair of the virtuous dispel;
for why should they?

4. (a) Let those whose conduct is like that of cranes and cats depart; (b) let the noble royal ministers of peaceful disposition remain; (c) let those who are clever in the art of buffoonery like the *ḍiṇḍika* stand aside.
(d) One may desire honey free from flies; but whence can there be a gathering of rogues?
(a) Ascetics do not attain liberation through weeping.
(b) Joking conversation does not obstruct the attainment of heaven;
(c) therefore, one with a clear mind should certainly laugh; (d) indeed, a wise person should abandon the *kaurukucī* mode of livelihood.

What indeed is this sound that is heard as if someone were making a request while I am preoccupied with my own petition? (Listening) Ah, I have understood! This is that rogue Cākrika, the bald Śyāmilaka, who, having entered the bower of creepers, strikes the bell and proclaims: "This is the secret of the pleasure of union for lovers... [p.67] 6 (a)... the distinction of the bliss of union for those filled with desire.
(b) A messenger of the time of day, a herald for the drums;
(c) at dawn, his [sound] is sweet, yet because of its harshness it is not followed by lions, (d) whose donkeys bray loudly in imitation.
Moreover, what is being proclaimed by him? (Listening) (Behind the scenes):
Victorious is the banner of Love, as the playful woman prepares for her beloved!
(b) Her foot, with its lac-dyed anklets, must be entreated with bowed head.
(Exit.)
(Stage direction) (Then enters the Libertine.
Libertine: Hold on now, sir! What is it that must be proclaimed here, such that this is being done?
(a) By one who, intent on a lovers' quarrel,
has revealed the root of her thighs by letting her garment slip; (b) she has indeed been conquered by the intoxication of passion.
"By whom was this laughed at with a foot jingling with anklets?
(Looking) "Dadruṇamādhava is also right here! "O Dadruṇamādhava, what is there to laugh at here? What do you say?"

"I witnessed it myself yesterday, when the venerable Viṣṇunāga, the vintner, was graced by the touch of the lotus-feet of the illustrious Madanasenikā, the chief courtesan of Surāṣṭra, who was full of passion.
Indeed, this is well said: 'Joy comes to a living man even after a hundred years.'"

"Even Viṣṇu-nāga—how can you say this? Has he not indeed received upon his head such a consecration known as the 'treading of the feet,' common to all those who desire love? What do you say? Whence could he have such good fortune as to become the recipient of such festivals of amorous quarrels? For that was a special mark of honor from her, the deity of the brothel."

Considering this an insult, his eyes reddened with rage, his forehead furrowed by a quivering frown, he shook his head, bit his lip with his teeth, struck his hand against his hand, sighed deeply, and said: "Alas! Shame on you, you unchaste woman, you who know not yourself!"
By you,
with hands purified, my mother carefully tied my topknot;
while I was bowing at her feet, my father smelled my head, saying, "This child is virtuous."
(c) Upon his head, which had been sprinkled by twice-born men with water for peace containing flowers and *lavaka* grass, he placed his foot; out of pride, no respect was shown to him at all.
And as he spoke thus, the night—like a twilight whose passion has faded—underwent a change of color, bearing a face as lusterless as the moon at the break of dawn. 10 (a)

With her pride and passion vanished, her graceful deportment falling away, her entire slender frame perspiring from despair as she wondered, "What is this?", her beauty dissipated by fear, with flowers vomited from her head.
(d) But saying "No more," she clung to his feet and bowed down in prostration; he shook her off and said, "O woman, do not touch me!"
"It is a pity, sir, that you should not deign to approach me because of my lowly birth!
Indeed, the female cuckoo follows the owl; even Madanasenikā follows that wretched, impotent male-vetāla—this is what causes me wonder—and yet he is the son of a high official!"

"Being appointed to carry out the king's commands, he neglects those who desire gifts; indeed, these women are seekers of fame. For it is taught that there are many kinds of purposes regarding desire. What do you say? 'Indeed, by seeking fame as one whose primary aim is fame, she has incurred the ruin of her reputation'—for she is truly a poor soul."
(a) With the lashes of her eyelids cast obliquely downward, (b) with the falling tears from her eyes washing her lips, breasts, and face,
(c) she suddenly hid herself within her own limbs, which were trembling anew.

(d) "She has been made to tremble by the clouds, like a royal swan"—this is not at all surprising, nor has it been heard by us who have already understood the matter; yet you ask about what is past. What do you say next? Then, having rebuked him, I said:
"O you wretched grammarian!"
"Do not crush the *sumanasa* flowers with a pestle; do not play the lute with a firebrand;

do not cut the delicate sprouts of the beautiful woman with the razor of speech. Though addressed thus, he disregarded me and went to the house of the eminent courtesan Bhaṭṭijīmūta. Then that poor woman, resting her face upon her sprout-like hand, began to weep. I raised her up and said: "O beautiful one,"

A monkey does not deserve a turban, nor is a donkey capable of pulling a magnificent carriage; enough with this weeping! This poor wretch is indeed laughable; he does not deserve such great honor for his head. (a) Is it not the case that lustful women, when intoxicated, forcibly afflict him by seizing him by the hair?
(b) He whom they do not bind with girdles, nor strike with ear-lotuses;
(c) for that fortunate man, Love is a festival and youth is a celebration;
(d) by him, women—having cast aside their modesty—play like a servant in secret.

Having spoken thus, she accepted my words with a sidelong glance preceded by a smile; then, covering her head and feet with her garment, she adorned the surface of the bed. I too, reflecting upon the misconduct of that inferior lover, passed the night. Thus, awakened by the sounds of the king’s morning benedictions, I performed my duties and beheld that very same evil dream.

Having gone to the Brāhmaṇa-pīṭhikā to dispel that [doubt], I saw upon that Brāhmaṇa-pīṭhikā Viṣṇugama himself, who had previously arrived there with disheveled hair and in a state of distress, proclaiming his own deed: "O sirs, I am such a man of such deeds; may these elders learned in the three Vedas deign to protect me, whose head was kicked by the feet of a low-caste woman. Thus he spoke.
The Brahmins, having looked at one another with smiles indicated by their quivering cheeks and having meditated for a moment as it were, said:

"O good sir, we have examined the Dharmaśāstras of the great sages such as Manu, Yama, Vasiṣṭha, Gautama, Bharadvāja, Śaṅkha, Likhita, Āpastamba, Hārīta, Pracetas, Devala, Vṛddhagārgya, and others; yet [we find] nothing of this kind in them."
When he was thus addressed, "We wish to know the expiation for this sin," his face became even more dejected; raising his hands, he cried out in lamentation:
"O, O! You gods upon earth, you ought not to abandon me simply because I am of the fourth caste. Why?
(a) I am noble, I am of pure conduct, and I am born of a high lineage."
(b) I have exerted myself in grammar and in the conventions of logic; (c) I am a servant of the king's command, not an ordinary person;
(d) Save me, for I am afflicted and without refuge—I have come to you for protection!
When she had spoken thus, in that assembly:
(a) some, thinking "This is a cow," struck one another with their arms as if they were not jewels; (b) others, with smiling faces, stood for a long time watching her, thinking, "She must be mad."
(c) By some, she was reviled as a "demoness of lust" and treated with contempt as if she were mere straw;
(d) by others, that very same woman was mourned as a perpetrator of evil deeds.
And while she remained in such a state, the Brahmins in that assembly were bewildered as to how to respond, and agitated by their uncertainty regarding the appropriate expiation.

While Viṣṇu-nāga was crying out, one among them, the teacher’s son— and the teacher himself, who was thoroughly trained in the science of government (*daṇḍanīti*), metaphysics (*ānvīkṣikī*), and other branches of knowledge, having attained supreme skill even in all the arts, eloquent,
surrounded by a circle of disciples, and a Brahmin named Bhavasvāmin Śāṇḍilya by nature inclined toward jesting— [raised] his right arm.

Raising his hand, he addressed the assembly with a voice brightened by a smile and said: "O Viṣṇunāga, do not fear; enough, enough with this despondency! There is this declaration of Dharma: 'The laws of country, caste, family, sacred sites, and conventions are authoritative when they are not in conflict with the traditional scriptures. Therefore, having assembled the guild of courtesans, [I shall prescribe] an expiation for the chief courtesans."

"Let them be sought out, for they will indeed release you from this transgression. When this was said, a procession of shouts of "Bravo! accompanied by the dancing of raised fingers broke out. Having heard that in that assembly, even the serpent Viṣṇu had been favored, he departed.
And as for you, you too have been appointed to the task of a gathering of libertines; certainly so. What do you say? Who, then, are the libertines here?
"You are indeed considered a *viṭa*! he said. "What do you mean by saying, 'How is it that even I am favored with the title of *viṭa*'?
What doubt could there be about this? Listen:
having spent the entire day in debate with litigants..."
(b) Having eaten your meal at the close of day in the house of some friend, (c) you take your pleasure at night with the women of the brothel and even cast away your weapons;
(d) yet there is not even water in your dwelling, and nevertheless you boast.
"How is it that you, being no *viṭa* yourself, say this: 'If you are thus favored and will assemble the *viṭas*, we wish first to hear the characteristics of a *viṭa*'? "Let the first rule be heard:
(a) He who protects his friends from calamities even at the cost of his own life;
(b) for whom, when he is in distress, his own arm—armed with a sword—is his sole refuge."

(c) He whom the assembly of courtesans seeks out due to rivalry and the affliction of passion, (d) he who has squandered his wealth and is constantly [at the disposal] of supplicants— such a person is to be known as a *viṭa*.
17. He whose head is honored by the pair of lotus-feet of beautiful women, who bears it like a crown out of satisfaction,
and whose wealth is enjoyed— he is proclaimed a "vita" by those who know the *vitas*.
(d) Like those afflicted by thirst, they take it with both hands as if it were water;
what do you say? You have described the characteristics of a libertine (*viṭa*); now you should instruct us regarding libertines themselves—listen:
There, the venerable Bhānu acts according to his own will;
Lomaśa is the minister Gupta Viṣṇudāsa;
and Śaibya is Āryarakṣita.
Dāśeraka Rudravarmā of Avantī, Skandasvāmī,
Hariścandra the physician, and Kumāra Mayūradatta the Ābhīra.
Mārdaṅgika, Sthāṇu, Gāndharvasenaka—
who was constantly engaged in the narration of propitiatory rites—
the Pārvatīya, Makhavarmā, the prince and first ruler of Aparānta from Ānandapura, Indravarman; and Kumāra.
Saurāṣṭrika Jayanandaka, Maudgalya Dayitaviṣṇu, and others like them should be assembled as appropriate. What do you say?
"Let all that wait for a moment; even Dayitaviṣṇu is considered a *viṭa* by you."
"What doubt is there? "What do you say? This is that very one who is appointed over the king's forces, the Pāraśava named Kavi.
"Certainly, it is even so. "What do you say? 'O sir, let it be so!
He who shrinks back even when his friendship with the king has been established...'"
(b) he who sleeps and awakens to auspicious signs;
(c) who, from worshipping the gods, is perfumed with the fragrance of guggulu resin;

(a) from the temple to the royal palace, and from the royal palace back again to the temple;
(b) thus pass the days of one who is excessively attached to these two families.
"How is it that he too is a *viṭa*? "Indeed, it is so; yet this quality of his is contrary to the nature of a *viṭa*, like the scent of old ghee. However:
(a) formerly in Avantī, during a brawl in a brothel, the tips of his hands were severed like branches; (b) in battle at Padmanagara, two arrows were driven into his thighs by his enemies."

(b) Even one whose senses have faded delights in conversations of love;
(c) therefore, I place him at the head of the foremost of libertines;
(d) for passion, not power, colors those who possess wealth—how could he not be a libertine?

(d) Along with the Mahiṣakas, Colas, Pāṇḍyas, and Keralas, [he says], looking: "Ah! Who indeed is this who approaches right here in a white palanquin from which the curtain has been removed, imitating the grace of a recently widowed woman? (Reflecting) Very well, I have recognized him; for he is that minister Viṣṇudāsa, a man of vulgar cleanliness, indicated by his staff and water-pot."

For by him, though appointed to such a great task as that of a judge, royal affairs were not conducted with excessive zeal, as if he were a monk dwelling in equanimity due to his devotion to the practice of meditation; thus,
with his knees slightly trembling from the movement of his hands, while some sat upon half-seats—
(b) With some bowing their heads, he has his feet pulled [toward them];

(c) even when presiding over legal cases, while litigants cry out, (d) like a bull in a marketplace, he meditates and falls asleep. Thus, his very sight is contrary to the desires of the profligate; nevertheless, what recourse is there for one who approaches him seeking instruction in Dharma?

I shall approach him. Indeed, having seen me from afar, he has alighted from his palanquin and is descending. Ah, sir! May you forgive us; you ought not to deprive us of our company by such formal constraints. What do you say? "Who is it that attends upon you? This is merely a custom we are following. Pray, do not speak thus while attending upon me in this manner.

Is it indeed fitting for you to thus turn away the noble Anaṅgasenā, who was so inclined toward you with affection, as if she were not Anaṅgasenā? What do you say? "Did I not show her a reception worthy of her affection? Behold, for by me—"
26. (a) After she had said "Svasti" and performed her salutation, (b) while she was seated, the Yogaśāstra was recited; (c) and her eyes were being moved as if by the wind.

[79] (d) Having observed her, he said, "Daughter, drink ghee. How is it that she was not accepted by me? Oh, what a charming way of accepting a gift from a lustful woman! He greets me with a smile and tries to appease me with this "pure" offering, a citron (*bījapūraka*). Ah, sir! We are indeed your own disciples; we cannot be deceived by such ruses as "not-to-be-opened" gifts in matters like this at all... Let it be so then. I shall depart for now. (Walking about.)
O sir, this great roar has reached the marketplace of the sovereign, where men from many regions have arrived for the purchase and sale of the finest goods produced on land and in water;
it is a tumultuous sound amidst the throngs of people, like the gathering of birds in their nesting places or the lowing of cattle in their pastures.
For thus:
(a) the vowel, together with its nasalization, falls into the marketplace of the artisan; (b) the bell-metal, mounted upon the lathe, produces sounds like the cries of ospreys.
(c) The weapon held in the conch shell resounds, portending the neighing of horses;
(d) and now, people obtain both purchase and sale on every side.
29. (a) These *sumanas* flowers are being sold, as if smiling with their beauty;
(b) the drinking cup moves through the taverns and is drunk from there;
(c) it is gazed upon askance by those who sell meat, holding grass in their hands.
(d) These city-birds fly even toward the slaughterhouse garlanded with swords;
and (a) they strike shoulder against shoulder, quarrel, and barter here and there.
(b) These crowds of men are moving like rows of ripening grain;
(c) these gamblers, having won a *māṣaka* from the game of dice, go toward their lodgings;
(d) they have arrived with their attendants, carrying flowers, cakes, meat, and spirituous liquors.
Therefore, let me now likewise leave this market street, which is difficult to traverse due to the crush of the great multitude, and instead take this flower-paved path,
turning to the right past the taverns, descending at the Pūrṇabhadra crossroads, and entering the quarter of courtesans by way of Makararathyā;
for that would be like the entrance of a courtesan’s quarter for one who has not yet gathered his wealth, or like a warrior’s descent into battle unarmored.

Thus, both [of these courses] are useless, leading only to infamy and misfortune; nevertheless, this command of our friend must certainly be carried out by us, especially since there will be a gathering of libertines at the *bhūyādveśa*. (Walking about) Ah!
Who indeed is this person accompanied by Rohitakīya drummers, with their bronze vessels and flutes, and the Yaudheya...?

Being sung to by bards, with a *kuraṇṭaka* flower garland hanging from one ear, repeatedly adjusting his upper garment— which was loosely draped over his right shoulder and disarrayed at its ten-fold border— with a handkerchief, and repeatedly exposing one buttock as he lifted the wine vessel with his left hand,
he makes the drinking pavilion resound with laughter while dancing. (Observing him closely)
Ah! Now I understand. This is indeed that son of a Bāhlīka, that rooster of a brothel, Bāṣpa, the rogue, who has become the sole object of the ridicule of all scoundrels.
Truly, I have never seen him even once without being intoxicated or drunk;
and yet, his hand remains untainted by even half a māsaka. How, then, could this [wealth] possibly belong to him? (Reflecting)

Ah, it is understood. For this man is forward, devoid of shame, and all-devouring due to his universal popularity; he has taken a handful of side-dishes while those [who had] formed a circle were drinking.
(31) (a) Of those who had formed a circle;
(b) while they were drinking.
(c) Steam enters the middle.

(d) Among the actors, actresses, servants, and horse-keepers—oh, indeed, what skill he possesses in earning his livelihood by drinking! Enough of this conversation; let us depart from here. (Walking about.)

This is another moving example of a decayed garden belonging to a libertine: for here is that ancient courtesan named Dharaṇīguptā, having fulfilled a vow made to the deity in the temple of Kāmadeva, placing her mass of hair—white as a withered kāśa creeper and fallen from the region of her shoulder—upon one shoulder; she wears a freshly washed lower garment and has cast off her upper cloth.

While composing herself, she cast a sidelong glance at a dancing peacock surrounded by crows that had descended upon the scattered offerings; then, circumambulating the dolphin-shaped pillar, she said: "O, it is true that even now her long-past youthful charm speaks of the remnants of her grace, for thus it is:"
(a) Her breasts, with their roots turned upward, are encircled by rows of white nail-marks;
(b) her lower lip, previously sucked dry, hangs loose between her slackened corners of the mouth;
(c) even now, because of our intimacy, she utters well-reasoned replies accompanied by a knitting of the brows.
(d) For although her form has been forcibly struck down by old age, her charms have not been taken away;

therefore, it is not possible to pass her by without speaking to her. For she, identifying herself as a friend to our dear companion the drummer Sthāṇumitra, reveals her own use of the *krauñca* elixir—how then [can we leave her]?

I shall approach her. (Reflecting) Ah, I have understood! For on the third day from now, the ascetic Sthāṇumitra, through excessive kissing, will experience such loathsomeness—oh, shame! Passion is merciless. (a) He is enamored of kissing her.
A tooth that had become loose fell from his own mouth;
having touched the root of his tongue,
he spat it out with a "khāṭ" sound.

[84] "I might well be deceived by attempting to enter this courtesan's quarter while passing by this gateway; nevertheless, the falling of her teeth upon the face of Sthāṇumitra has been made manifest. Therefore, I shall not cause my shame to be redoubled by approaching her.
In every way, salutations to her! I shall depart. (Walking about.)

I have indeed entered this pleasure-house; oh, what supreme splendor belongs to this pleasure-house! For here—these various structures are situated separately, crowded with palaces, mansions, turrets, pigeon-cotes, *siṃhakarṇa* spires, *gopānasī* rafters, *valabhī* roofs, inner chambers, watchtowers, gateways, and balconies; their courtyards are well-arranged and undisturbed, their divisions well-planned, and they are adorned with beautifully constructed moats, filled and sprinkled water-channels, hollows, whistling pipes, raised platforms, plastered surfaces, and paintings of both minute and large distinct forms.
Hundreds of palaces were built, with their joints, doors, windows, balconies, courtyards, walkways, and turrets firmly joined;
their central areas were adorned with one, two, or three pillars; they were beautified by designated trees, groves of green fruit-bearing trees, and clusters of garlands;

furthermore, I perceive from their qualities that the monkey-dancer is a lover from Mālava and the singer is a donkey—in every way, I understand them to be common [in nature]. Indeed, the Creator is truly skilled in matching like with like; for instance: [The verse continues: The Yavana woman, the dancer-monkey, the Mālava lover, the donkey-singer— I recognize them as equal by virtue of their qualities; in every respect, the Lord of Creatures is indeed expert in joining similar things. Thus it is.
116. (a) The *ātmaguptā* creeper has taken refuge upon a *khadira* tree; (b) it clings to a *nimba* tree—alas, what a union!
If the Yavanī is attached to Mālava,
then let this friend of mine have her will;
however, I shall not speak to her, for who indeed would address such sounds as these, which abound in hissing and resemble the chirping of female monkeys?

He will hear certain other matters, indicated merely by the caressing of her forefinger—matters whose specific details are not to be recognized—which she herself has related to the courtesan Veśayavanī; so enough of this.
(Walking about) Who is this other person?

It has been learned that this son of a merchant, known by the common name Viṭapravāla among the *ḍiṇḍis*, is the lord of those whose garments are as tattered as rags used for crossing the ocean of amorous play;
overcome by passion, he has disregarded the commands of his father and mother and become enamored with that courtesan, our daughter.
Indeed, this is truly an excessive boast; we are merely those who have been shrouded by the title of "father-in-law. Enough of this conversation!

Here is my salutation with joined palms. Now, let us depart from here—(walking about)—while I too go to the assembly of libertines. Here I am, sirs, at the great thoroughfare of the brothel, which has been passed by in vain, belonging to the chief of libertines.

Having reached the residence of Bhaṭṭijīmūta—a place whose courtyard gates were crowded by thousands of attendants and mounts gathered from all sides, and where gateways were attended by servants holding up silver pitchers for washing the feet—he thought: "Truly, it is well said that the undertakings of the great are indeed great;
for now these five-colored flowers are being carved out, released, attached, woven, and arranged."
Incense is burned, lamps are lit, a welcome is proclaimed, a vehicle is displayed, a diversion is provided, song is sung,
music is played, a hand is offered, gentle words are spoken, a smooth embrace is given,
an affectionate hold is maintained, a respectful bow is made, a modest touch is applied, and one who has bowed is smelled upon the back with a raised eyebrow.

The head is held with graceful movement; one sits down with playful charm; sandalwood is distributed; unguent is applied; cosmetic paste is laid on; powder is sprinkled; jests are exchanged by the *viṭas*; and they are received by the wanton women—what more need be said? (118a) These flowers have become entangled, reaching as high as the knees.
(b) With difficulty, their feet are lifted by the dwarfs;

Moreover, these leading courtiers— (a) illustrious, with half their seats adorned by their companions,
and (b) performing clever jests that do not pierce the vital spots.
(c) Approached on all sides by courtesans, (d) these bulls appear like those in a pen surrounded by cows;
moreover, this is their assembly hall.
(a) Like the sky with a hundred moons, [the place was filled] by the moon-like faces of the women;

(c) it was as if possessed by youths through the collisions of their arms.
(d) Even with chests moistened by sandalwood paste, as if piled up with stones, these courtesans shine here like wish-fulfilling trees.
(a) These courtesans shine here like kalpavṛkṣas.

(b) Indeed, those heroes who, even in their childhood, spoke of wooden quarrels as if they were real, (c) and whose elders recounted them loudly like the [fights] between Suyodhana and Vṛkodara; (d) such men are both impetuous for the moment and ruinous to their foundations.

Therefore, having placed my head at the feet of the venerable Lord of the Mind to carry out the command of my friend, and honoring this office by my friend's instruction, I announce to the rogues for the sake of expiation, preceded by the proclamation of the illustrious Viṣṇunāga of Tuṇḍikera: (walking about) Ho there! "He calls me here; here I come. What does my lord command?—I have heard this before, yet you speak it again. 128. (a) May he never win a stake in gambling;

(Looking around) Here is Dhārāyaka, whose story is endless; having risen suddenly, he calls out to me. What do you say? "This is the transgression of that very woman who did not understand his affection; your honor ought not to hear it. (A) He who, by his touch, causes the Aśoka tree to blossom out of season.
(b) Upon which [foot] Kama himself dwells, with his bow and arrows drawn;
(c) that very foot was placed by her upon the head of a beast as if out of delusion; (d) surely let that same fickle woman perform penance for a very long time!
You have spoken correctly; for indeed,
(a) this donkey has been serenaded by lute,
and (b) this monkey has been celebrated in song.
(c) This [milk] has been boiled in buffalo milk; (d) the juice of the mango has been poured in.
Nevertheless, expiatory rites are prescribed for those who are afflicted, and this person has arrived in a state of affliction.
Therefore, your honors ought to show him favor. Now, where indeed is this grandson of Gogla?—

this man who, having seized with one hand his head that was shaken by the impetuosity of intoxication, and having wiped the region of his forehead with his forefinger— which is covered with drops of sweat like scattered small pearls— listen to his penance.

Just as he calls me, I approach; meanwhile, these parasites—what is this man here whose appearance is defiled by the nature of a parasite? "Indeed, let the honorable sirs speak:

(c) Having placed my son, a crying infant, (d) I drank wine together with a maidservant. "How could I be a non-profligate?"—if they acknowledge you in this way, saying, "You are a chief among profligates," then sit down. What do you say?

"What else may I bring you that would be pleasing? Listen, sir:

(c) May there be many meetings with beloved gallants in this city; (d) may there be many nights at twilight, great festivals of love with courtesans.

Thus ends the Bhāṇa named *Pādatāḍitaka*, the work of the poet Ārya Śyāmilaka, a northerner and son of Viśveśvaradatta.
